“Whoever they are,” he eventually intones, “they were here first, and we are here now, and shame on us. Good?”It’s an amusing bit, and when I attended a recent preview, it further piqued my curiosity about the show, which I hadn’t seen during its previous run.
If you love musicals and/or theater and satire or absurd comedy, this show is for you.
Slam Frank takes aim at every ideology in sight, and its willingness to offend everyone equally makes it the most daring ticket Off-Broadway this fall.

“Slam Frank” mostly succeeds in satirizing the state of the mainstream American theater, which is inexplicably hell-bent on reimagining decades-old shows written by and for white people with BIPOC casts rather than supporting new work written by artists of diverse backgrounds.

The way Slam Frank chooses to address it is quite possibly the most shocking thing I've ever seen in a New York theater.
The cast is extraordinary. The score is terrific. The book needs clarity. The premise remains difficult for me to accept, yet, would I tell you to see it? Absolutely.

cn.t: This audacious Anne Frank satire divides critics with its provocative lampoon of contemporary theater and identity politics. Most praise its subversive ambition and talented cast, though some question whether its boundary-pushing offense serves a clear purpose.

vr.q: The show is funny. The show is subversive. The show is one of a kind and I think that is the reason to go see this.
